headline: Mice get better at fighting just by watching

sources.title: Mice can learn to fight by watching tiny rodent cage matches, study finds (NPR)
Mice that watch fights come away battle-ready (Princeton University, EurekAlert!)
What Happened When Neuroscientists Started a Mouse Fight Club (Nautilus)

chunks.text: Male mice that only watched other mice fight became better fighters themselves, according to a new study. [[Brain scientists]] at Princeton University in New Jersey published the study in the journal Nature on November 4, 2026. They wanted to {{find out}} what animals can learn just by watching others. The team {{split the mice up}} into three groups: fighters, [[spectators]] and beginners. Each group had eight days of [[training sessions]].

verbs.correct: To learn a fact you did not know
verbs.wrong: To guess the answer to a question
verbs.why: Students find out their test scores on Friday. Parents often find out about school news from their kids. The scientists wanted to find out what animals can learn just by watching others.

verbs.correct: To divide people or animals into groups
verbs.wrong: To choose the strongest of a group
verbs.why: The coach splits the class up into two teams. Our teacher splits us up into groups of four. The team split the mice up into three groups: fighters, spectators and beginners.

chunks.text: The fighters had short [[practice fights]] with a weak mouse. The spectators sat on a [[raised platform]] behind a [[clear barrier]]. From there, they watched fights between other mice {{play out}} below. They could see, hear and smell the action, but they could not {{join in}}. The beginners {{missed out on}} the fights. Instead, they played with a [[stuffed toy]]. On the ninth day, every mouse faced a tough [[opponent]] in three short [[rounds]].

verbs.wrong: To stop for a short rest
verbs.why: Fans watch the big game play out on TV. A good movie lets the story play out slowly. The spectators watched fights between other mice play out below.

verbs.correct: To do an activity with others
verbs.why: My little brother always wants to join in when we play cards. Anyone can join in the dancing at the end of the party. The spectators could see, hear and smell the action, but they could not join in.

verbs.correct: To not get to do something others do
verbs.wrong: To lose a fight by a small amount
verbs.why: Kids who stay home sick miss out on the class trip. Late guests often miss out on the best food. The beginners missed out on the fights and played with a stuffed toy instead.

chunks.text: All that watching {{paid off}}. The spectators and the fighters were quicker to [[attack]] the tough opponent than the beginners. They also {{backed away}} less often and spent less time with their [[backs turned]]. But no group spent more time attacking than the others. The scientists say watching made the mice better prepared, not more [[aggressive]]. The [[senior author]] said the spectators were about [[halfway]] between beginners and experienced fighters.

verbs.why: Hard work at school usually pays off. Practice pays off when you play a new song well. All that watching paid off when the spectators faced a tough opponent.

verbs.correct: To move backward to avoid a threat
verbs.wrong: To make a loud sound at a rival
verbs.why: A cat backs away when a big dog barks at it. Most people back away from a snake on the path. The spectators backed away less often than the beginners did.

chunks.text: The scientists also studied cells in 12 [[brain regions]]. The team changed some cells so they would {{light up}} when active. Over the eight days, cells that act like a [[brake]] on fighting {{eased off}} in both fighters and spectators. When the team {{brought back}} the brake's full strength, the mice fought like beginners again. The senior author said people also {{pick up}} [[skills]], like sports moves, by watching others. But it is not clear how much of the mouse study {{carries over}} to humans.

verbs.correct: To start to glow or shine
verbs.why: The city streets light up at night. The screen lights up when a message arrives. The team changed some cells so they would light up when active.

verbs.wrong: To send a message to the body
verbs.why: The pain in my back eases off after a hot shower. The wind usually eases off in the evening. Cells that act like a brake on fighting eased off in both fighters and spectators.
The new coach brings back the old team rules. Many towns bring back their summer fair after a bad year. When the team brought back the brake's full strength, the mice fought like beginners again.

verbs.wrong: To score high on a skills test
verbs.why: Children pick up new words from their parents. Many people pick up a little Spanish at work. The senior author said people also pick up skills, like sports moves, by watching others.

verbs.correct: To apply in a different situation
verbs.wrong: To be tested on animals first
verbs.why: Good habits at home often carry over to school. Skills from one sport sometimes carry over to another. It is not clear how much of the mouse study carries over to humans.

mainIdea.s: Male mice that only watched other mice fight did better in their own fights later. Their brains also changed in ways that looked partly like the brains of mice with real fighting experience.
mainIdea.why: All that watching paid off, since the spectators were quicker to attack a tough opponent. Brain cells that act like a brake eased off in them too.

mainIdea.s: Mice that watched fights from behind a barrier grew meaner and attacked much more often than the others. Scientists say watching made them angry, so their brains could no longer stop a fight.
mainIdea.why: Close, but no group spent more time attacking than the others. The spectators were better prepared, not more aggressive, and only about halfway to real fighters.

mainIdea.s: A new study finds that pet mice sleep longer when their cages are kept dark and quiet at night. Researchers in Utah say owners should also give each mouse a small box where it can hide.
mainIdea.why: This study is about mice that watched other mice fight. Scientists wanted to find out what animals can learn just by watching others.

tf.s: The scientists wanted to find out what animals learn by watching others.
tf.why: They wanted to find out whether mice could learn just by watching, so some mice only watched fights.

tf.s: The spectator mice were allowed to join in the fights they watched.
tf.why: They watched from behind a clear barrier. They could see, hear and smell the action, but they could not join in.

tf.s: Watching fights made the spectator mice much more aggressive.
tf.why: No group spent more time attacking than the others. The watching paid off by making the mice better prepared, not more aggressive.

tf.s: Brain cells that act like a brake on fighting eased off in the spectators.
tf.why: Over the eight days, these cells eased off in both the fighters and the spectators.

tf.s: Scientists say the mouse results clearly carry over to people.
tf.why: It is not clear how much of the mouse study carries over to humans.

tf.s: Mice can pick up fighting skills just by watching other mice.
tf.why: The spectators picked up skills by watching and were quicker to attack a tough opponent than the beginners.

lines.text: Did you see the study about mice that watched other mice fight?
No. What did the scientists want to {{find out}}?
Whether animals can learn just by watching. They {{split the mice up}} into fighters, spectators and beginners.
So the spectators had a [[front-row seat]]?
Pretty much. They watched the fights {{play out}} from behind a clear wall, but they couldn't {{join in}}.
They {{missed out on}} the fights. They just played with a stuffed toy.
Poor guys. So did all that watching {{pay off}}?
It did. The spectators were quicker to attack a tough mouse, and they {{backed away}} less.
So they can [[learn the ropes]] without ever fighting.
Right, but they weren't more aggressive. They were just better prepared.
Kind of. One scientist said the watchers were only about [[halfway there]] compared to real fighters.
Some cells work like a brake, and they {{ease off}}. When the team {{brought back}} the brake, the mice fought like beginners again.
Do people {{pick up}} skills that way too?
Some, like sports moves. But nobody knows how much of this {{carries over}} to humans.
Still, I feel better about all the hours I spend watching basketball.

expressions.def: An advantage that helps someone begin before or better than others
ex: Reading to kids gives them a head start at school.

expressions.def: Used to say that someone has done about half of what is needed
ex: I've saved 500 dollars, so I'm halfway there.
